If You Only Remember These

  1. First-line drugs = HRZE — Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide. Streptomycin is excluded from first-line, moved to 2nd-line or Category II retreatment use. p.1-2
  2. New TB, drug-sensitive (Category I): 2HRZE/4HR — 2 months intensive phase (HRZE) then 4 months continuation phase (HR), regardless of bacteriologic status. p.15
  3. Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by KatG (mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase), the active form inhibits InhA and blocks mycolic acid synthesis. Bactericidal, works even against resistant strains of other drugs. p.2-3
  4. Rifampicin binds the beta-subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB gene) and blocks mRNA synthesis. It is a strong CYP450 enzyme inducer and colors body fluids orange-red. p.4
  5. Pyrazinamide is a prodrug converted by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (pncA) to pyrazinoic acid, only active in an acidic, intracellular environment. It is the most hepatotoxic first-line drug and causes hyperuricemia in essentially all patients — this is expected and not itself a reason to stop the drug. p.5-6
  6. Ethambutol is bacteriostatic, blocks arabinosyl transferase (embCAB operon), and its hallmark toxicity is dose-related optic/retrobulbar neuritis with red-green color blindness. Not used in young children who cannot report visual changes. p.6
  7. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) is given with isoniazid to prevent and treat peripheral neuropathy, the drug's most common benign adverse effect. p.3-4
  8. Hepatotoxicity stop-rule: discontinue all anti-TB drugs if ALT is more than 3x ULN with symptoms, or more than 5x ULN even without symptoms. p.13, 23
  9. A patient is bacteriologically confirmed if AFB is found by smear, culture, or Xpert MTB/RIF — one positive sputum smear is sufficient. p.1-2
  10. MDR-TB = resistant to at least isoniazid AND rifampicin. RR-TB (rifampicin-resistant, isoniazid status unknown or sensitive) is managed as MDR-TB per WHO. p.8-9
  11. The newer, WHO-preferred regimen for MDR/RR-TB is BPaLM — Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid + Moxifloxacin, for 6 months, replacing the older 9 to 24-month regimens. p.22
  12. In HIV patients on TB treatment, Efavirenz is the preferred NNRTI — avoid Nevirapine due to drug interactions. p.12, 19
  13. ART timing: start 2 weeks after TB treatment begins regardless of CD4 count, EXCEPT in TB meningitis, where ART waits until after the 2-month intensive phase. p.12, 19
  14. Rechallenge = incremental dosing, fewer doses, shorter duration, more commonly used in the Philippines. Desensitization = incremental dosing, higher doses, longer duration, contraindicated in SJS/TEN or mucosal involvement. p.13-14
  15. Second-line drugs fall into WHO Groups A to D — A: fluoroquinolones, B: aminoglycosides, C: other core oral agents, D: add-on agents (D1 first-line add-backs, D2 bedaquiline/delamanid, D3 PAS/carbapenems). p.7, 24
  16. Linezolid inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, watch for serotonin toxicity with SSRIs and for thrombocytopenia beyond 2 weeks of use. p.11
  17. Bedaquiline and Delamanid both cause QT prolongation — get a baseline ECG before starting, in addition to ALT/AST/uric acid/creatinine. p.22-23
  18. Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside given only IM, never crosses the BBB, and its hallmark toxicities are ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and rare neuromuscular blockade. p.7
  19. Latent TB infection (LTBI) regimen used in the Philippines is 3HR (3 months isoniazid plus rifampicin) — monotherapy with isoniazid alone (6H or 9H) is also acceptable because of the low bacillary load. p.18-19
  20. Serum uric acid and routine LFTs are not requested before starting TB drugs in asymptomatic patients without risk factors — testing is triggered only by symptoms. p.19, 23

High-Yield Topic Sections

Tuberculosis — Overview and Diagnosis p.1-2 reviewed

Core idea: TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slow-growing acid-fast bacillus (AFB) first isolated by Robert Koch in 1882. The Philippines is one of the WHO's 22 TB "high burden" countries worldwide.

Must Know
  • Why mycobacteria are intrinsically drug-resistant: they grow slower than other bacteria and multiply inside macrophages (drugs effective on rapidly growing cells work poorly), they can become dormant (resistant to many drugs, killed only slowly), and their lipid-rich cell wall is impermeable to many agents.
  • Rationale for TB treatment: (1) chemotherapy of active disease, (2) chemoprophylaxis to prevent infection or symptom manifestation in infected individuals.
  • Bacteriologically confirmed TB = AFB detected by smear microscopy, culture, or a WHO-approved rapid diagnostic test (Xpert MTB/RIF). One (1) positive sputum smear is sufficient where External Quality Assessment (EQA) is well established (Strong R, moderate QE).
  • Clinically diagnosed TB = does not meet bacteriological confirmation criteria, but a clinician gives a full TB treatment course based on x-ray, other imaging, or suggestive histology. If later found bacteriologically positive (before or after treatment starts), reclassify as bacteriologically confirmed.
  • 2013 WHO case definitions —
    • New case: never treated for TB, or has taken TB drugs less than 1 month
    • Retreatment case: received at least 1 month of TB drugs in the past, whether completed, discontinued, or lost to follow-up, or failed treatment after 5 months with unknown outcome
    • Relapse: previously treated, completed treatment, now has a recurrent episode
    • Treatment after failure: previously treated, recently declared a treatment failure (at month 5)
    • Treatment after lost to follow-up (TALF): interrupted treatment for 2 consecutive months
    • Previous Treatment Outcome Unknown (PTOU): previously treated, most recent outcome unknown or undocumented
Should Know
  • Common sites of infection: apical areas of the lung (oxygen-rich, TB bacilli are aerobic — no predilection for a particular side), renal parenchyma, liver parenchyma, GIT tissue, growing ends of bones.
  • Identifying presumptive TB — cough of at least 2 weeks duration (Strong R, Low QE), unexplained cough of any duration in a close contact (Strong R, Low QE), or CXR findings suggestive of PTB with or without symptoms (Strong R, Low QE). A weaker basis (Weak R, Low QE) is any of: cough of any duration, unintentional weight loss, fever, hemoptysis, non-musculoskeletal chest pain, fatigability/malaise, night sweats, or dyspnea.
  • Non-infectious criteria — bacteriologically confirmed, no DR-TB risk factors: at least 14 daily doses of treatment plus sputum conversion plus clinical improvement. Clinically diagnosed, no DR-TB risk factors: at least 5 daily doses plus clinical improvement.
Nice To Know

M. tuberculosis multiplies within macrophages, which prevents lysosomal degradation and allows survival, leading to granuloma formation. A patient's history and physical exam should also cover previous TB treatment, hepatic/renal/ocular toxicity risk factors, sexual history, occupation, and personal/social history (Strong R, moderate QE).

memory aid, not in PDFA simple way to keep the case definitions straight: "New" = never or under a month. Everything else with prior treatment is some flavor of "Retreatment."
Recall Check
What single lab result is enough to call a PTB case "bacteriologically confirmed"?
One positive AFB sputum smear (Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence), assuming EQA is established in that lab.
A patient completed TB treatment before, then interrupted a new course for 2 straight months before resuming. What is this called?
Treatment after lost to follow-up (TALF), a subtype of retreatment case.
First-Line Drugs — Overview and Category I Basics p.2, 14 reviewed

Core idea: First-line drugs are used for new or newly diagnosed TB cases. Second-line drugs are commonly given for multidrug-resistant strains.

Must Know
  • Current first-line drugs: Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), Ethambutol (E), Pyrazinamide (Z). Streptomycin is excluded from the modern first-line list because of high resistance incidence and numerous adverse effects, and has been transferred to the second-line drugs / used as a retreatment option.
  • Basic principles of TB treatment: (1) multiple drug regimen — monotherapy is never advocated, use an armamentarium of drugs, (2) drug administration must continue for a sufficient period, (3) aim for the most effective therapy in the shortest period of time.
  • Isoniazid + Rifampin alone for 9 months cures 95 to 98% of cases. Adding Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol for the first two months allows the total duration to be shortened to 6 months — this is why HRZE for 6 months is the commonly used Philippine regimen.
Should Know
  • Recommended treatment of pulmonary TB in general is 6 months of a combination of drugs.
  • If a retreatment case tests negative for multidrug-resistant TB, the Category 1 approach can still be used — Category 1 treatment can be given to both newly diagnosed AND retreatment cases, provided the case is not multidrug-resistant.
Source Inconsistency Worth Knowing

Early in the PDF, the "Category 1 treatment" continuation phase is listed as Isoniazid, Rifampin, Ethambutol (3 drugs). Later, in the synchronous-session slides (used as the explicit answer key for a case question), the confirmed DOH Category I regimen is 2HRZE/4HR — a continuation phase of Isoniazid + Rifampicin only, without Ethambutol. The PDF does not reconcile these two statements. Because the synchronous session explicitly tested and confirmed 2HRZE/4HR as the answer, treat 2HRZE/4HR as the exam-safe default for a new drug-sensitive case unless a question specifies otherwise.

Recall Check
Which first-line drug from the classic list is no longer considered first-line today, and why?
Streptomycin — excluded due to high resistance incidence and numerous adverse effects, now used as a 2nd-line / retreatment component.
Isoniazid (INH) p.2-4, 18, 20 reviewed

Core idea: The most active drug for TB caused by susceptible strains. A small, water-soluble molecule structurally very similar to pyridoxine. Bactericidal for actively growing tubercle bacilli, but less effective against atypical mycobacterial species.

Must Know
  • MOA: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by KatG (mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase). The activated form forms a covalent complex with an acyl carrier protein (AcpM) and KasA, and forms an isonicotinoyl-NAD adduct that inhibits InhA (an NADH-dependent enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase). This blocks mycolic acid synthesis, an essential mycobacterial cell wall component. Effect: bactericidal.
  • Resistance mechanisms: mutation or deletion of katG, overexpression of inhA, overexpression of ahpC (an oxidative-stress protection gene), and mutation in kasA. Resistant mutants exist at baseline in about 1 in a million bacilli — since a tuberculous lesion often has more than 100 million bacilli, monotherapy readily selects out resistant organisms.
  • Must be co-administered with Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) to prevent peripheral neuropathy, its most common benign adverse effect, especially in malnutrition, chronic alcohol use, HIV, pregnancy, breastfeeding, renal failure, or diabetes.
  • Isoniazid-induced hepatitis is the most common MAJOR toxic effect (distinct from minor asymptomatic AST/ALT rises), can be fatal especially over age 50. Clinical hepatitis (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, RUQ pain) occurs in about 1% of recipients. Risk rises with age: rare under 20, 0.3% at 21-35, 1.2% at 36-50, 2.3% at 50 and above.
  • Peripheral neuropathy is dose-related, occurs in 10-20% of patients on more than 5 mg/kg/day, and is more common in slow acetylators.
Should Know
  • PK: readily absorbed from the GIT (Tmax 1-2h), diffuses into ALL body fluids and tissues including CSF (20-100% of serum levels), pleural/ascitic fluid, placenta, and breast milk. Metabolized by hepatic acetylation via NAT2 (genetically determined) — fast acetylators have a shorter half-life (about 1 hour, or 30 min to 2h per one table) and lower plasma levels, slow acetylators have a longer half-life (about 3 hours or more). 75-95% excreted in urine. No dose adjustment needed in renal failure.
  • Other ADRs: elevated LFTs, aplastic anemia (rare), hypersensitivity reactions, drug-induced SLE (rare), dark urine, fever, and skin rash.
  • Drug interactions: Isoniazid inhibits hepatic metabolism of carbamazepine, ethosuximide, phenytoin, diazepam, triazolam, and clofazimine, and inhibits cycloserine and warfarin metabolism — this raises levels/toxicity risk of those drugs. It increases metabolism of enflurane. Aluminum hydroxide (antacids) inhibits INH absorption.
  • Reduced bioavailability with food — best taken on an empty stomach.
  • Use in pregnancy: not known to have harmful effects, pyridoxine supplementation recommended for all pregnant or breastfeeding women taking it.
Nice To Know
  • First made in the early 20th century, activity against TB first reported in the early 1950s, marketed in 1952. On the WHO List of Essential Medicines.
  • In vitro, inhibits most tubercle bacilli at 0.2 mcg/mL or less.
  • Can be given IM or IV at the same dosage as oral if needed.
  • Dosing note: the PDF gives slightly different pediatric dosing across two tables — an early table lists "children 10-30 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses," while the later synchronous-session table lists "children 10-15 mg/kg not exceeding 300 mg/day, or 20-40 mg/kg not exceeding 900 mg given 2-3 times weekly." Both are reproduced here as written rather than reconciled.
  • Latent TB / monotherapy dosing: adult 300 mg/day (5 mg/kg/day) for 9 months, children 10 mg/kg/day. This is one situation where isoniazid monotherapy is acceptable, because the bacillary load is low.
Mechanism
Isoniazid (prodrug)
↓ activated by KatG (mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase)
Nicotinoyl radical (activated drug) + NAD+
↓ spontaneous
Nicotinoyl-NAD adduct — inhibits InhA
↓
Mycolic acid synthesis blocked
↓
Bactericidal cell wall damage (rapidly-growing bacilli)
Common Confusion (brief — full version in Confused Concepts section)

Isoniazid inhibits hepatic metabolism of drugs like phenytoin and carbamazepine (raising their levels toward toxicity), while Rifampicin induces hepatic metabolism of many drugs (lowering their levels toward subtherapeutic / breakthrough effect). These are opposite directions of effect on the same class of co-administered drugs.

Recall Check
Which enzyme activates isoniazid into its active form?
KatG, the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase.
What enzyme does activated isoniazid inhibit, and what pathway does this block?
InhA (an enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase), which blocks mycolic acid synthesis.
A 16-year-old on Category I treatment develops tingling and heaviness in the limbs. What should be given?
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) — this is isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy (Clinical Case 4).
Fast acetylators vs slow acetylators — who is more prone to peripheral neuropathy on isoniazid?
Slow acetylators, because they maintain higher circulating isoniazid levels for longer.
Rifampicin (Rifampin) p.4-5, 16, 20-21 reviewed

Core idea: A semi-synthetic derivative of Rifamycin B, a macrolytic antibiotic produced by Streptomyces mediterranei. Discovered 1957, marketed 1971. On the WHO List of Essential Medicines.

Must Know
  • MOA: Rifampin binds the beta-subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB gene product), inhibiting initiation of the RNA chain and thus RNA/protein synthesis. Effect: bactericidal against rapidly dividing mycobacteria. Human RNA polymerase does not bind rifampin, which is why it is selectively toxic to bacteria.
  • Resistance: point mutations in the rpoB gene reduce rifampin binding.
  • Rifampin readily penetrates most tissues and phagocytic cells, and can kill organisms poorly accessible to other drugs, such as intracellular organisms and those sequestered in abscesses and lung cavities.
  • Strong CYP450 (CYP3A4) enzyme INDUCER — decreases levels of many co-administered drugs: oral contraceptives, dapsone, protease inhibitors, sulfonylureas, steroids, ketoconazole, calcium channel blockers, oral anticoagulants, benzodiazepines, acetaminophen, clofibrate, doxycycline, levothyroxine, nortriptyline, tacrolimus, zidovudine, hydantoins (phenytoin), sulfa drugs, enalapril, and carbamazepine.
  • Hallmark ADRs: cholestatic jaundice/hepatotoxicity, and orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears (can permanently stain soft contact lenses) — this discoloration also serves as a marker of drug adherence.
  • Used in pregnancy — give Vitamin K at birth to the infant of a mother taking rifampicin, because of the risk of postnatal hemorrhage.
Should Know
  • PK: well absorbed orally (food reduces absorption by about 30%, so take on an empty stomach), Tmax 2-4h, half-life 2-5h (about 3h per one summary table). Widely distributed, crosses the BBB but only reaches adequate CSF levels if the meninges are inflamed (as in TB meningitis). Hepatic deacylation to an active metabolite, mostly biliary excretion with enterohepatic recirculation, less than 30% urinary excretion. No renal or hepatic dose adjustment usually necessary.
  • Other ADRs: flu-like syndrome if dosed less often than twice weekly (fever, chills, myalgia, anemia, thrombocytopenia), light-chain proteinuria, and occasionally hypersensitivity, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute tubular necrosis, or nephritis.
  • Other indications: eliminate meningococcal carriage (600 mg twice daily x 2 days), Haemophilus influenzae B prophylaxis in child contacts (20 mg/kg/day x 4 days), and serious staphylococcal infections such as osteomyelitis or prosthetic valve endocarditis, in combination with other agents.
  • Must always be given with isoniazid or other anti-TB drugs to prevent emergence of drug-resistant mycobacteria — never as monotherapy for active disease.
  • Dosing: 10 mg/kg once daily, max 600 mg/day, for 6 months in combination. As a single drug alternative to isoniazid for latent TB (if isoniazid cannot be taken): 600 mg daily for 4 months.
Nice To Know

Active in vitro against gram-positive and gram-negative cocci, some enteric bacteria, and chlamydiae. Susceptible organisms inhibited by less than 1 mcg/mL. Resistant mutants exist at baseline in about 1 in a million organisms.

Common Confusion — Rifampin vs Rifaximin
Rifampin
Anti-TB drug / antimicrobial. Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Rifaximin
Used for hepatic encephalopathy, by decreasing ammoniagenic bacteria in the gut.
Fast distinction: if the question is about TB, it's Rifampin. If it's about ammonia/liver encephalopathy, it's Rifaximin.
Mechanism
Rifampicin binds β-subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB)
↓
Blocks initiation of the RNA chain (inhibits mRNA synthesis)
↓
Bactericidal against rapidly dividing mycobacteria (human RNA polymerase unaffected)
Recall Check
What gene mutation causes rifampin resistance?
rpoB — the gene for the β-subunit of RNA polymerase.
Name two body fluids that turn orange-red with rifampin use.
Urine and tears (sweat also — and it can permanently stain soft contact lenses).
Why doesn't rifampin harm human cells even though it blocks RNA polymerase?
Human RNA polymerase does not bind rifampin — selective toxicity for the bacterial enzyme.
Pyrazinamide (PZA) p.5-6, 16, 21 reviewed

Core idea: A relative of nicotinamide and a close structural analog of isoniazid. Stable, slightly soluble in water. A prodrug. On the WHO List of Essential Medicines.

Must Know
  • MOA: Pyrazinamide is converted by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (encoded by pncA) to its active form, pyrazinoic acid. It is inactive at neutral pH but active at acidic pH (about 5.5) — the drug is taken up by macrophages and acts within the acidic environment of lysosomes. The protonated pyrazinoic acid permeates the mycobacterial membrane and lowers cytoplasmic pH, disrupting basic chemical processes, especially energy production. It also targets Fatty Acid Synthase I and interferes with NAD as an ETC cofactor. The exact drug target itself is not fully known.
  • Overall the drug is largely bacteriostatic, but can be bactericidal against actively replicating TB bacteria, provided the environment is acidic.
  • Resistance: impaired uptake of pyrazinamide, or mutation in the pncA gene that impairs conversion to the active form.
  • Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic of all first-line drugs — hepatotoxicity occurs in 1-5% of patients along with nausea, vomiting, and drug fever.
  • Hyperuricemia occurs uniformly / is expected on PZA — this is NOT itself a reason to halt therapy. It may provoke acute gouty arthritis, which IS managed (see Adverse Reactions section).
  • Drug interaction: Allopurinol, probenecid, and colchicine all decrease PZA levels. If gout or joint pain develops from PZA-induced hyperuricemia, colchicine or allopurinol can be used to help taper symptoms.
Should Know
  • PK: well absorbed orally, Tmax 2h, half-life 9-10h. Widely distributed including inflamed meninges with high CSF penetration, which is why it is important for treating meningeal TB. Hepatic metabolism, renal excretion (about 70% in urine, 3-4% unchanged). In hemodialysis patients, dose 25-35 mg/kg three times weekly (not daily), since metabolites are renally cleared even though the parent compound is hepatically metabolized.
  • Other ADRs: arthralgia, myalgia, gout, minor rash, photosensitivity, sideroblastic anemia.
  • Precautions: careful glucose monitoring in diabetes (levels can become labile), can exacerbate gout, monitor LFTs where possible, ESRD dosing is 3x weekly. Can probably be used safely in pregnancy using the same 6-month regimen (based on isoniazid safety data).
  • Absorption is unaffected by food (unlike isoniazid and rifampicin, both reduced by food).
Nice To Know

Inhibits tubercle bacilli in vitro at approximately 20 mcg/mL at pH 5.5. Active both intracellularly and, per one summary table, also described as targeting mycobacteria "intracellularly" specifically in the acidic environment of lysosomes — the PDF's cheat sheet lists PZA's site of action simply as "intracellular."

Exam Trap

Asymptomatic hyperuricemia on pyrazinamide is expected and is NOT a reason to stop the drug or to routinely test uric acid. Uric acid testing is only triggered by symptoms of gouty arthritis (Strong R, Low QE).

Mechanism
Pyrazinamide (prodrug)
↓ hydrolyzed by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (pncA)
Pyrazinoic acid (active form)
↓ only active in an acidic, intracellular environment (macrophage lysosomes)
Protonated pyrazinoic acid permeates membrane, acidifies cytoplasm
↓
Disrupts membrane transport / Fatty Acid Synthase I / NAD-dependent ETC
↓
Bacteriostatic overall (bactericidal only vs actively replicating bacilli in acidic conditions)
Recall Check
What enzyme activates pyrazinamide, and what gene encodes it?
Pyrazinamidase, encoded by pncA.
At what pH is pyrazinamide active against tubercle bacilli?
Acidic pH (about 5.5) — inactive at neutral pH.
True or false: asymptomatic hyperuricemia on PZA should prompt stopping the drug.
False — it is expected and only symptomatic gouty arthritis warrants action.
Of the four first-line drugs, which is most hepatotoxic?
Pyrazinamide.
Ethambutol p.6-7, 17, 21 reviewed

Core idea: A synthetic, water-soluble, heat-stable compound discovered in 1961. The (+) enantiomer is used because it is more effective. On the WHO List of Essential Medicines.

Must Know
  • MOA: inhibits the enzyme arabinosyl transferase, encoded by the embCAB operon, which blocks arabinogalactan (polymer) synthesis, an essential mycobacterial cell wall component, and increases cell wall permeability. Effect: bacteriostatic against actively growing TB bacilli (susceptible strains inhibited at 1-5 mcg/mL).
  • Resistance: mutations causing overexpression of emb gene products, or mutations within the embB structural gene.
  • Hallmark ADR: dose-related optic neuritis / retrobulbar neuritis, causing loss of visual acuity and red-green color blindness. Risk is higher at 25 mg/kg/day continued for months, and rare at 15 mg/kg/day or less. Discontinue ethambutol immediately if visual impairment develops, and refer to ophthalmology.
  • Contraindications: known hypersensitivity, and pre-existing optic neuritis from any cause. It is relatively contraindicated in young children who cannot reliably report changes in visual acuity or color perception.
Should Know
  • PK: 75% oral absorption, Tmax 2-4h, half-life 3-4h. Well distributed but penetrates the CSF inconsistently — crosses the BBB only when the meninges are inflamed. Less than half is metabolized. About 50% excreted unchanged in urine, 20% in feces — accumulates in renal failure (dose reduced by half if creatinine clearance is under 10 mL/min, and given 3x weekly rather than daily if creatinine clearance is under 30 mL/min).
  • Other ADRs: peripheral neuropathy, hyperuricemia, and rarely rash, arthralgia, or hepatitis. Hypersensitivity is rare.
  • Drug interactions: alcohol, antacids, allopurinol, probenecid.
  • Per the lecture's cheat sheet, ethambutol promotes early sputum conversion and delays resistance when combined with the other first-line drugs.
  • Use in pregnancy: not known to be harmful.
Nice To Know

Dosing: 15 mg/kg (range 15-20) daily, or 15-30 mg/kg (max 2 g/day) once daily in combination, or 25-35 mg/kg (about 30 mg/kg) three times weekly in intermittent regimens.

Source Inconsistency Worth Knowing

The PDF states two different pediatric age cutoffs for ethambutol contraindication in different places — the main adverse-effects discussion says "contraindicated in children below 6 years," while a later summary table (Table 24) says "CI in children less than 5 years old." Both numbers are reproduced here as written since the PDF does not reconcile them — the safest exam framing is simply that ethambutol is avoided in young children too young to reliably report visual changes.

Common Confusion — Ethambutol vs the other first-line drugs

Ethambutol is the only bacteriostatic drug among Isoniazid, Rifampicin, and Pyrazinamide (all bactericidal by the cheat sheet's classification, with the nuance that PZA is only bactericidal under acidic conditions). Its site of action is unique too — it targets arabinogalactan synthesis (cell wall), not mycolic acid synthesis (Isoniazid) or RNA polymerase (Rifampicin) or intracellular acidification (Pyrazinamide).

Recall Check
What enzyme/operon does ethambutol inhibit?
Arabinosyl transferase, encoded by the embCAB operon.
What visual finding is classic for ethambutol toxicity?
Loss of visual acuity and red-green color blindness (retrobulbar/optic neuritis).
Is ethambutol bactericidal or bacteriostatic?
Bacteriostatic.
Streptomycin p.7, 21 reviewed

Core idea: An aminoglycoside antibiotic, historically the first clinically useful drug against TB. No longer considered first-line.

Must Know
  • Bactericidal. MOA: irreversibly binds the 16S component of the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting mycobacterial protein synthesis.
  • Must be given IM only — it is not absorbed from the GIT.
  • Active only against extracellular bacilli in an alkaline pH — this is essentially the opposite niche of pyrazinamide (intracellular, acidic pH).
  • Does not cross the BBB.
  • Hallmark ADRs: ototoxicity (vestibular disturbance / gait disturbance is the major concern), nephrotoxicity (minimal), and rare neuromuscular blockade.
  • Now excluded from first-line use, due to high resistance incidence and numerous adverse effects — used in second-line regimens or Category II retreatment where locally available (for example within 2HRZES/1HRZE/5HRE).
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation.
  • If ototoxicity develops → stop streptomycin, refer to ENT. If nephrotoxicity develops → stop streptomycin, refer to nephrology.
Should Know
  • PK: poorly absorbed from the GIT (hence IM only), therapeutic concentrations reached in bile, pleural fluid, and extracellular fluid. CSF concentration reaches about 20% of serum levels only with meningeal inflammation. Excreted primarily unchanged by the kidneys.
  • Facial paresthesia occurs in about 15% of patients (tingling of the hands), occasional hypersensitivity.
  • Drug interactions: high-dose aspirin, concomitant diuretics (potentiate toxicity).
  • Resistance: mutational changes in the ribosomal binding protein, or one-step mutation / plasmid acquisition. Isolates resistant to streptomycin are NOT cross-resistant to amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin — always use drug-resistance / culture-guided testing rather than assuming class-wide resistance.
Nice To Know

Also used for endocarditis and plague, outside the TB indication.

Recall Check
Why must streptomycin be given IM rather than orally?
It is poorly absorbed from the GI tract.
In what pH and cellular location is streptomycin active?
Alkaline pH, extracellular bacilli only.
A patient on Category II treatment develops hearing loss and tinnitus with no history of trauma. Which drug is responsible?
Streptomycin (ototoxicity) — Clinical Case 3.
DOH/WHO Treatment Regimens — Categories and Resistance Patterns p.7-9, 15-16 reviewed

Core idea: The PDF presents two overlapping ways to classify TB regimens — by DOH treatment Category (new vs retreatment, and site of disease), and by drug-resistance pattern (drug-sensitive, mono-resistant, poly-resistant, rifampicin-resistant). Both frameworks are reproduced here since the source uses both.

Must Know — DOH Treatment Categories (Table 21, synchronous session)
CategoryIndicationRegimen
Category INew Pulmonary TB, Miliary TB, New EPTB (except CNS/bones/joints)2HRZE/4HR
(WHO alternative: 2HPZM/2HPM, 4-month regimen — not always available due to limited resources)
Category IaNew TB of CNS / bones / joints2HRZE/10HR
Category IIRetreatment of Rifampicin-susceptible PTB and EPTB (except CNS/bones/joints)2HRZES/1HRZE/5HRE,
or 2HRZE/4HR (if Gene Xpert susceptible, no culture resistance),
or 2HRZE/7HRE,
or 2HPZM/2HPM (WHO)
Category IIaRetreatment of Rifampicin-susceptible TB of CNS, bones, or joints2HRZES/1HRZE/9HRE

Suffixes: H = Isoniazid, R = Rifampicin, Z = Pyrazinamide, E = Ethambutol, S = Streptomycin. Prefix number = months of that phase. IP = Intensive Phase, CP = Continuation Phase.

Must Know — Regimens by Drug-Resistance Pattern
PatternDefinitionIntensive PhaseContinuation Phase
Monodrug-resistant TBResistant to ONE first-line drug (Isoniazid, Ethambutol, or Pyrazinamide) but NOT RifampicinRifampicin + two 1st-line drugs + one injectable 2nd-line drug + one fluoroquinolone daily, x3-6 monthsInjectable stopped, remaining 4 oral drugs continued x9-12 months
Poly-drug-resistant TBResistant to MORE THAN ONE first-line drug, but NOT to both Rifampicin AND Isoniazid togetherRifampicin + one injectable 2nd-line drug + one fluoroquinolone + any 1st-line drug, x3-6 monthsInjectable stopped, remaining 3 oral drugs continued x9-12 months
Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB)Resistant to Rifampicin, Isoniazid sensitive or unknown — WHO treats this as MDR-TB(6-9) Kanamycin, Levofloxacin, Ethionamide, Cycloserine, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol, high-dose Isoniazid → (18) Levofloxacin, Ethionamide, Cycloserine, Ethambutol, high-dose Isoniazid. Can run up to 2 years by this classic protocol (shorter options discussed in the 2nd-Line and 2024 WHO Updates sections).
Exam Trap

Don't confuse "poly-drug-resistant TB" with "MDR-TB." Poly-DR-TB is resistant to more than one first-line drug but specifically NOT to both Rifampicin and Isoniazid together. MDR-TB specifically requires resistance to both Isoniazid AND Rifampicin.

Should Know
  • The administration of drug-resistance-pattern regimens still follows DOTS treatment principles, similar to the usual intensive-phase course and Category I regimen for susceptible strains.
  • If a retreatment case is Gene Xpert-susceptible with no culture resistance, the original 2HRZE/4HR regimen may still be given in the local (DOH) setting — an important nuance for Category II decision-making.
Recall Check
What is the DOH Category I regimen for a new pulmonary TB case?
2HRZE/4HR.
What distinguishes poly-drug-resistant TB from MDR-TB?
Poly-DR-TB is resistant to more than one first-line drug but not to both rifampicin and isoniazid together. MDR-TB requires resistance to both.
How is rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) managed according to WHO?
As MDR-TB.
Second-Line Drugs and MDR-TB — Classification and Regimen Building p.7-9, 22, 25 reviewed
Must Know — When to Suspect and How to Manage DR-TB
  • Suspect DR-TB in: all retreatment cases (relapse, treatment failure, TALF, PTOU) (Strong R), and new cases who are non-converters to Category I, contacts of confirmed DR-TB cases, or PLHIV with signs/symptoms of TB (Strong R, High QE).
  • Diagnosis: Xpert MTB/RIF is the required initial test in presumptive DR-TB (Strong R, High QE) — faster than conventional phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) on culture, though culture DST remains the more thorough reference method. Line probe assay (LPA) is another genotypic option.
  • Management: ALL DR-TB patients must be managed under a programmatic setting — refer immediately to the nearest PMDT Treatment Center, Satellite Treatment Center, or DOTS facility with PMDT services (Strong R, High QE). Management outside this framework only leads to further drug resistance.
Must Know — WHO Categorization of 2nd-Line Drugs (Chart 1)
GroupClassDrugs
Group AFluoroquinolonesLevofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Gatifloxacin (not on the market)
Group BAminoglycosidesAmikacin, Capreomycin, Kanamycin, (Streptomycin — significant resistance, not recommended)
Group COther core second-line agentsEthionamide/Prothionamide, Cycloserine/Terizidone, Linezolid, Clofazimine
Group D1Add-on, first-line agentsPyrazinamide, Ethambutol, high-dose Isoniazid
Group D2Add-on, newer agentsBedaquiline, Delamanid (approved but still under investigation)
Group D3Add-on, other agentsPara-aminosalicylic acid, Imipenem+cilastatin (requires clavulanate), Meropenem (requires clavulanate), Amoxicillin+clavulanate, Thioacetazone (not for use in people living with HIV)
Must Know — Stepwise Regimen Building (Lecturer's Cheat Sheet)
STEP 1 — Use any available first-line agents the isolate is susceptible to (Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) + one Fluoroquinolone (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin) + one Injectable agent (Amikacin, Capreomycin, Kanamycin, Streptomycin)
↓
STEP 2 — Add oral second-line drugs until you have 4-6 drugs total (optimally at least 5) to which the isolate is susceptible, preferably ones not previously used in this patient (Cycloserine, Ethionamide, PAS, Linezolid)
↓
STEP 3 — If 4-6 drugs are still not available from the categories above, consider third-line drugs in consultation with an MDR-TB expert (Bedaquiline, Delamanid, Clofazimine, Imipenem, Meropenem/Clavulanate, Amoxicillin/Clavulanate, Clarithromycin, high-dose Isoniazid)

Per the lecturer: Meropenem is used if no Bedaquiline or Delamanid is available. Clofazimine is also used in leprosy. Carbapenems are reserved for truly drug-resistant cases — used cautiously since they are also important for other types of antimicrobial resistance, not just TB.

Should Know — Older Classification (Groups I-V)
GroupCategoryDrugsCharacter
IFirst-line oral drugsIsoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, EthambutolMost potent, best tolerated, routine use
IIInjectable drugsStreptomycin, Kanamycin, Amikacin, CapreomycinPotent, bactericidal, injectable
IIIFluoroquinolonesOfloxacin, Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, CiprofloxacinBactericidal, oral, given for MDR-TB
IVSecond-line oral drugsEthionamide, Prothionamide, Cycloserine, Terizidone, PAS, Rifabutin, RifapentineLess effective, bacteriostatic, toxic oral drugs
VUnclear efficacy drugsBedaquiline, Clarithromycin, Clofazimine, Linezolid, Co-amoxiclav, Imipenem/cilastatinUncertain efficacy, not for MDR-TB, reserve drugs, for XDR-TB

Per the lecturer: "Groups are numbered as such because when treating MDR strains there is a stepwise manner of addition of medications that we follow. There are no specific groups of drugs that must be used, and these drugs can be used in combination."

Nice To Know

Short-course (Bangladeshi protocol) MDR-TB regimen — 4 months of Kanamycin, Moxifloxacin, Prothionamide, Clofazimine, high-dose Isoniazid, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, then 5 months of Moxifloxacin, Clofazimine, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide. This shortened the classic up-to-2-year regimen. It has since been further shortened by the 2024 WHO BPaLM regimen (see the 2024 WHO Updates section).

Recall Check
What is the required initial test for all presumptive DR-TB cases?
Xpert MTB/RIF.
Which WHO group includes Bedaquiline and Delamanid?
Group D, specifically D2.
According to the lecturer, must the numbered Groups I-V be followed as strict, separate treatment categories?
No — they reflect a stepwise order of addition, drugs can be combined, and there is no rigid requirement to use a whole group.
Individual Second-Line and Novel Drug Profiles p.9-11, 22-23 reviewed

Full numeric details (dose, half-life, metabolism) for each of these are also collected in the Master Tables section — this card focuses on MOA, hallmark ADRs, and interactions.

Should Know — Aminoglycosides (Amikacin, Kanamycin, Capreomycin — Streptomycin covered separately)
  • Bactericidal, inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis at the 30S subunit.
  • Poorly absorbed from the GIT (parenteral only). CSF concentration reaches about 20% of serum only with meningeal inflammation.
  • ADRs: facial paresthesia (~15%), ototoxicity (vestibular disturbance is the major concern), minimal nephrotoxicity, rare neuromuscular blockade.
  • Streptomycin resistance does NOT cross-react with amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin resistance — culture-guided, drug-specific resistance testing is needed.
Should Know — Rifamycins: Rifabutin and Rifapentine
  • Bactericidal, block DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (same class mechanism as rifampin), lipophilic and longer-acting.
  • Clinical uses: prevention and treatment of TB, and treatment of MDR-TB.
  • ADRs: GI intolerance, orange-red discoloration of secretions. Resistance: mutation in rpoB.
  • Rifapentine specifics: used in the LTBI regimen "3HP" (once-weekly Isoniazid + Rifapentine, less hepatotoxic than 9H), dosed at 900 mg once weekly for LTBI, or 1200 mg/day in the 4-month WHO regimen for active TB (see 2024 WHO Updates). Bioavailability ~70% (higher with a high-fat meal), cannot cross the BBB, half-life 17 hours (long), hepatic ester metabolism to an active metabolite, mostly fecal excretion (70%), highly protein bound (not removed by dialysis). Baseline AST monitoring — discontinue if AST rises more than 5x. Reduces levels of statins, oral anticoagulants, OCPs, glucocorticoids, amiodarone, thyroid hormone, and several HIV medications (ritonavir, indinavir, saquinavir, efavirenz, delavirdine) via CYP450 interaction.
Nice To Know — Ethionamide and Cycloserine
  • Ethionamide: bacteriostatic, MOA relatively unknown but proposed similar to isoniazid (with cross-reactivity to isoniazid). Less than 1% excreted as active drug, half-life 1.5-2h. Also used as an adjunct in Hansen's disease (leprosy). Teratogenic — contraindicated in pregnancy. Causes GI irritation and hepatotoxicity, needs renal dose adjustment.
  • Cycloserine: oral, bacteriostatic, inhibits peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis by targeting alanine racemase and D-ala-D-ala ligase. Cross-reactivity with isoniazid. Also used in Hansen's disease, active against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. ADRs: drowsiness, headache, fatigue, rash, and rarely psychosis, seizure, or coma. Isoniazid and ethionamide potentiate cycloserine toxicity (dizziness), and alcohol raises seizure risk. Per Katzung, it is produced by Streptomyces orchidaceous, distributes widely including into the CNS, and causes serious dose-related CNS toxicity (headache, tremor, acute psychosis, convulsions).
Should Know — Fluoroquinolones (class) and Moxifloxacin
  • Bactericidal, inhibit bacterial topoisomerase IV and DNA gyrase. Resistance via mutations in gyrA (and parC). Also effective against gram-negative organisms.
  • ADRs: photosensitivity, GI symptoms, seizures, prolonged QT interval. Reduce the therapeutic effect of phenytoin and probenecid. Use cautiously in the elderly (seizure risk, prolonged QT) and in cardiac disease.
  • Per Katzung: Moxifloxacin is most active against M. tuberculosis in vitro. Levofloxacin is slightly more active than ciprofloxacin against M. tuberculosis, while ciprofloxacin is slightly more active against atypical mycobacteria.
  • Moxifloxacin detail: 400 mg tablet or IV for TB. MOA targets DNA gyrase (Topo II) and Topoisomerase IV. Rapid absorption, ~90% bioavailability unaffected by food, ~50% protein bound, half-life ~12 hours. Limited hepatic metabolism to two inactive metabolites — sulfate M1 (fecal) and glucuronide M2 (urine). ADRs: tendon damage (sometimes overlooked), seizure risk, can worsen myasthenia gravis, can cause both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, and C. difficile-type diarrhea (as can clindamycin). Avoid combining with aluminum/magnesium antacids or zinc (reduced absorption) — the lecturer specifically warned about combining with vitamin C plus zinc supplements due to possible GI interaction.
Must Know — Linezolid
  • Bactericidal. MOA: inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit (binds the 23S rRNA portion).
  • A member of the oxazolidinone class (memory cue: "oxa" = oxazolidinone).
  • Also used against gram-positive bacteria including vancomycin-resistant staphylococci (VRSA).
  • ADRs: thrombocytopenia if given more than 2 weeks, rare hematologic toxicity.
  • Drug interaction: SSRIs (citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine) — increased risk of serotonin toxicity (headache, nausea, vomiting).
  • Resistance: mutation of the 23S ribosomal unit. Part of the new BPaLM regimen at 600 mg.
Must Know — Bedaquiline
  • Bactericidal. MOA: inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase — active against both replicating AND non-replicating (dormant) bacilli.
  • Bioavailability doubles when taken with food (peak plasma time 5 hours) — remind patients to take it after eating.
  • Dosing: Weeks 1-2, 400 mg (4x100 mg tablets) once daily. Weeks 3-24, 200 mg (2x100 mg tablets) three times weekly, totaling 600 mg/week.
  • ADRs: QT prolongation, vomiting, vertigo, arthralgia, rash, metallic taste.
  • Drug interaction: CYP3A4 inducers reduce levels — avoid or use cautiously with efavirenz or lopinavir-ritonavir in HIV-positive patients. Must be combined with at least 3 other active anti-TB drugs.
  • Get a baseline ECG before starting (not just ALT/AST/uric acid/creatinine).
Must Know — Delamanid
  • Bactericidal. MOA: inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (same target class as isoniazid, but a different activation pathway). Activated by enzyme Rv3547 (part of the F420-dependent bioactivation pathway).
  • Bioavailability increases with food, eliminated via the fecal route.
  • Dosing for MDR-TB: 100 mg BID x24 weeks, combined with other TB drugs.
  • ADRs: QT prolongation, nausea/vomiting, anorexia, fatigue, dizziness, headache, hemoptysis, increased blood amylase/transaminases, rash, arthralgia/myalgia, chest pain, dark/cola-colored urine, jaundice.
  • Drug interaction: CYP3A4 inhibitors — lopinavir, ritonavir, clarithromycin, amiodarone, quinidine.
  • Resistance: mutations in one of 5 genes in the F420-dependent bioactivation pathway.
Should Know — Pretomanid
  • MOA: inhibits mycolic acid synthesis — classified as a nitroimidazooxazine ("cousin" of Delamanid, which is a nitroimidazooxazole).
  • Dose 200 mg/tablet. High-fat/high-calorie meals improve absorption, time to peak 4-5h, lipophilic and crosses the BBB, steady state in 4-6 days, half-life 16-20h.
  • ADRs: hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy — the same toxicity family as isoniazid and ethambutol.
  • Part of the BPaLM regimen at 200 mg once daily (see 2024 WHO Updates).
Common Confusion — Delamanid vs Pretomanid
Delamanid
Nitroimidazooxazole. Activated by enzyme Rv3547.
Pretomanid
Nitroimidazooxazine — described in lecture as Delamanid's "cousin."
Fast distinction: both inhibit mycolic acid synthesis and share the toxicity family with isoniazid/ethambutol (peripheral/optic neuropathy), but they are chemically distinct compounds activated through different specific enzymes.
Recall Check
Which drug inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase?
Bedaquiline.
Which second-line drug's MOA is inhibition of the 50S ribosomal subunit, and what is it also used for outside of TB?
Linezolid — also used against gram-positive bacteria including VRSA.
Erika, a newly diagnosed MDR/RR-TB patient, is prescribed an oxazolidinone that is also used for VRSA. What is its mechanism?
Inhibits binding of mycobacteria to the 23S subunit (Linezolid) — Clinical Case 9.
Before starting bedaquiline or delamanid, what baseline test is essential beyond the usual liver/renal/uric-acid labs?
A baseline ECG, because both cause QT prolongation.
2024 WHO Updates — BPaLM and the 4-Month Regimen p.15-16, 22 reviewed
Must Know — BPaLM Regimen for MDR/RR-TB
  • WHO 2022 (referenced alongside ERS/ATS/CDC/IDSA 2024) suggests a 6-month regimen composed of Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid (600 mg) + Moxifloxacin (BPaLM), rather than the older 9-month or longer (up to 18-month) regimens, for MDR/RR-TB patients. (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence.)
  • Doses: Bedaquiline 400 mg once daily for 2 weeks then 200 mg three times weekly (or alternatively 200 mg daily for 8 weeks then 100 mg daily) — Pretomanid 200 mg once daily — Linezolid 600 mg once daily — Moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily.
  • BPaLM further shortens what the Bangladeshi protocol had already brought down to 9 months, versus the older regimens that could last 18 or even 24 months for MDR-TB.
  • WHO prefers BPaLM because all drugs are given orally. Not every DOTS clinic can offer it — it is more available at big or referral hospitals.
Must Know — 4-Month Rifapentine-Moxifloxacin Regimen (2HPZM/2HPM)
  • An option for pulmonary TB caused by organisms not known or suspected to be drug-resistant, for patients who are:
    • 12 years or older
    • Body weight at or above 40 kg
    • Living with HIV with a CD4 count at or above 100 cells/microliter, on (or planning to start) an ART regimen without known drug-drug interactions with this regimen
    • Free of contraindications to the regimen
  • Only an efavirenz-containing ART regimen may be combined with the rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen — other ART combinations carry drug-drug interaction risk.
  • Per WHO criteria, dosing is uniform across weight bands: Rifapentine 1200 mg/day, Moxifloxacin 400 mg/day.
Should Know — Weight-Band Dosing for the 4-Month HPZM Regimen (as given in the PDF)
Weight bandIsoniazidRifapentineMoxifloxacinPyrazinamide
40 to under 50 kg300 mg1200 mg400 mg1500-1600 mg*
50 to under 65 kg———1500-1600 mg*
65 kg and above———2000 mg

*Pyrazinamide dose depends on use of the 400 mg or 500 mg tablet formulation. The PDF's table only itemizes Isoniazid/Rifapentine/Moxifloxacin doses explicitly for the 40-under-50 kg row — the higher weight bands are shown in the source primarily for the Pyrazinamide component.

Exam Trap

Per the lecturer: "Questions in the exam will specifically indicate if the treatment basis is WHO (i.e., 'according to the WHO guidelines...'). Otherwise, if not specifically indicated, default to the DOH National TB Control Program Guidelines." In the Philippines, the default answer for PTB of any severity remains 2HRZE/4HR, not the newer 4-month or 6-month options, unless the question flags WHO criteria.

Nice To Know — Systematic Screening and Recognition

See the branching screening algorithm in the Mechanisms and Pathways section for the full decision flow used for adults 15 years and older with unknown HIV status.

Fixed-dose combinations available in the Philippines include Fixcom 2, Fixcom 4, and Quadmax (HRZE 75/150/400/275 mg). The number of tablets given per day is based on the patient's weight — for example, a 40 kg patient can receive 4 tablets/day for 2 months in the intensive phase, and in the continuation phase (HR 75/150 mg) a 65 kg patient can receive 5 tablets/day.

Recall Check
What 4 drugs make up the BPaLM regimen, and how long is it given?
Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin — for 6 months.
Which ART regimen is safe to combine with the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen?
An efavirenz-containing regimen only.
If an exam question doesn't specify WHO or DOH criteria, which should you default to?
DOH National TB Control Program Guidelines.
TB in Special Populations p.11-13 reviewed
Must Know — HIV (PLHIV)
  • Screening: ALL newly diagnosed PLHIV should be screened for active TB (Strong R, High QE).
  • Diagnosis: symptomatic screening (cough of any duration, fever, night sweats, weight loss) plus CXR and Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial test (Strong R, High QE). Refer to a DOTS facility with PMDT services or an Xpert facility before starting treatment. If Xpert is negative, base the diagnosis on a high index of clinical suspicion (Strong R, High QE).
  • Treatment: same regimen as the general population, PLUS Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis (800/160 double-strength) to prevent Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, regardless of CD4 count (Strong R, High QE).
  • ART timing: start ART after the second week of TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count — this spacing avoids worsening both diseases via immune reconstitution. Exception — TB meningitis: ART is started only after the intensive phase of TB treatment (the first 2 months). Total meningitis treatment runs 12 months (2 months plus 10 months). ART is free in the Philippines through HIV hubs.
  • Efavirenz is the preferred NNRTI for HIV patients on TB treatment — avoid Nevirapine due to drug-drug interactions (Strong R, High QE).
  • PLHIV with presumed DR-TB → refer immediately to PMDT treatment facilities (Strong R, High QE).
Should Know — Diabetes Mellitus
  • Screening for TB in people with DM "may be considered," given high TB prevalence in the Philippines (Weak R, Low-Moderate QE).
  • Treatment same as the general population (Strong R, High QE). Optimal glucose control is important since active infection can make blood sugar unpredictable (Strong R, High QE). Refer to a diabetes specialist if control is difficult.
Should Know — Solid Organ Transplant (SOT) and Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant (HSCT)
  • Work-up is the same as the general population.
  • Kidney and liver transplant candidates need dose adjustments based on drug and disease severity, and may need 3x/week dosing (Strong R, Moderate QE).
  • No DR-TB risk factors: 12-18 months of Isoniazid + Ethambutol (HE) (Weak R, Moderate QE).
  • Severe TB (disseminated, cavitary, bacteriologically positive): extended coverage, 6-11 months, 2HRZE/4-9HR (Weak R, Moderate QE).
Should Know — Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
  • First-line drugs with dose modification as appropriate. Second-line drugs adjusted per renal function (Strong R, High QE).
  • Timing: hemodialysis patients — give anti-TB medications immediately after a hemodialysis session. Peritoneal dialysis patients — anti-TB medications may be given regardless of PD schedule (Strong R, Low QE).
Must Know — Chronic Liver Disease (CLD)
  • Compensated cirrhosis: 2HRSE/6HR (8 months), or 2HSE/10HE, or 9HRE. Note that Streptomycin replaces Pyrazinamide in this regimen, because pyrazinamide's hepatotoxicity and arthralgia risk are unwanted in liver disease.
  • Decompensated cirrhosis: refer to a specialized center, because second-line TB drugs may be needed (Strong R, Low QE).
Must Know — Pregnancy and Lactation
  • Treatment is the same as the general population: HRZE + 4HR (2HRZE + 4HR).
  • Streptomycin is contraindicated in pregnant and lactating women.
  • Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation, 10-25 mg/day, is recommended to prevent peripheral neuropathy (Strong R, Moderate QE).
  • Isoniazid is not known to have harmful effects in pregnancy. Rifampicin requires Vitamin K at birth for the infant, due to postnatal hemorrhage risk.
Common Confusion — ART Timing, General TB vs TB Meningitis
General pulmonary/extrapulmonary TB
Start ART after week 2 of TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count.
TB meningitis
Start ART only after the 2-month intensive phase of TB treatment.
Fast distinction: meningitis waits for the whole intensive phase, ordinary TB only waits 2 weeks.
Recall Check
When should ART start in a PLHIV newly diagnosed with pulmonary TB (not meningitis)?
After the second week of TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count.
Which anti-TB drug is dropped and replaced by Streptomycin in compensated liver cirrhosis, and why?
Pyrazinamide — because of its hepatotoxicity and arthralgia risk.
Why give Vitamin K to a newborn of a mother on Rifampicin?
To prevent postnatal hemorrhage.
Adverse Drug Reactions — Recognition and Management p.12-14, 23 reviewed

Vignette (Case 6): Nilda, 65, diabetic, started Anti-Koch's regimen (4-tablet FDC) a week ago, develops abdominal pain and itchiness that worsens. She wonders if she should stop the drug. This illustrates a patient having an adverse reaction to TB medication — the framework below is how the lecture works through that.

Must Know — General Framework
  • ADR symptoms range from mild to severe (rash, anaphylaxis, serum sickness), and can be organ-specific or systemic.
  • Monitor ALT, AST, uric acid, and creatinine when indicated (symptom-triggered, not routine — see system-specific rules below).
  • Cutaneous manifestations are the most common presentation and the earliest sign of systemic drug allergy — some protein/polypeptide drugs can directly stimulate antibody production.
  • Drug Hypersensitivity Reaction = a severe, unexpected reaction affecting several organ systems at once. If accompanied by eosinophilia on CBC plus systemic symptoms not fully explained by TB itself, this can be considered DRESS (Drug Rash with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) or DIHS (drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome). Mechanism: delayed T-cell-mediated reaction — tissue damage from cytotoxic T cells and cytokine release. Management: STOP the medication first, wait until AST/ALT/creatinine/uric acid normalize and symptoms resolve, then do a rechallenge or desensitization.
Must Know — Minor vs Major ADR and General Management
CategoryExamplesManagement principle
MinorGI intolerance, mild/localized skin reactions, orange/red urine, injection-site pain, burning feet (peripheral neuropathy), arthralgia (hyperuricemia), flu-like symptomsSymptomatic therapy — first-line drugs should NOT be stopped without adequate justification
MajorSevere skin rash (hypersensitivity), jaundice (hepatitis), impaired visual acuity/color vision (optic neuritis), hearing impairment/tinnitus/dizziness (8th cranial nerve), oliguria/albuminuria (renal disorder), psychosis/convulsion, thrombocytopenia/anemia/shockALL drugs discontinued, may need single-drug formulations, refer to specialist

Per the lecturer: "All drugs are discontinued only when there is a major adverse drug reaction. Wait it out, then switch to fixed-dose combinations or a single-drug regimen using an incremental pattern of administration — this is rechallenge."

Must Know — Rechallenge vs Desensitization
FeatureRechallengeDesensitization
DefinitionProgressive dosing until full dose is reached, to verify no immediate reaction occursRapid administration of incremental doses to induce drug tolerance
Dose/durationFewer doses, shorter durationHigher doses, longer duration
Usage in the PhilippinesMore commonly used in clinical practiceUsed when rechallenge fails and the causative drug cannot be discontinued
ContraindicationsNone specifically listedSevere cutaneous reaction involving mouth/mucous membranes — SJS, TEN (exfoliative dermatitis)
Example sequenceDay 1: Isoniazid alone. Day 2: Isoniazid alone. Day 3: Isoniazid + half-dose Rifampicin. Day 4: Isoniazid + full-dose Rifampicin (by weight).—
Must Know — System-by-System Management
SystemWhen to testAction threshold / management
HepatotoxicitySymptoms (jaundice, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) OR baseline risk factors / abnormal LFTs 2-4 weeks after starting treatment. Routine LFT monitoring NOT needed if asymptomatic with no risk factors (Strong R, Moderate QE).ALT more than 3x ULN with symptoms, or more than 5x ULN without symptoms → stop ALL drugs immediately, evaluate promptly. Once ALT under 2x ULN AND symptoms resolved → reintroduce Rifampicin first, then Isoniazid after 3-7 days. Pyrazinamide is permanently discontinued if hepatotoxicity was prolonged or severe.
GI reactions—Mild → reassure, continue medications. Persistent → antacids. Taking with food is NOT recommended as first-line management.
Peripheral neuropathyNo labs needed — clinical monitoring for burning/numbness/tinglingTreatment: Vitamin B6 50-100 mg OD. Prophylaxis: Vitamin B6 10 mg OD. Risk factors: alcoholism, malnutrition, DM, HIV co-infection, slow acetylator phenotype, pregnancy, breastfeeding, renal failure.
Visual impairmentVisual acuity test + Ishihara color test if symptoms of ocular toxicity developDiscontinue Ethambutol if visual impairment develops, refer to ophthalmology.
OtotoxicitySymptoms of decreased hearing, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, or ataxia in a patient on StreptomycinStop Streptomycin, refer to ENT.
HyperuricemiaUric acid ONLY when gout symptoms develop — NOT routineDiscontinue PZA if gouty arthritis develops, give standard gout treatment (febuxostat or colchicine), refer to rheumatology if persistent.
Cutaneous reactions—Minor/limited rash → antihistamines, continue drugs. Generalized rash with fever and/or mucous membrane involvement → STOP ALL DRUGS immediately, refer to dermatology. Once improved, restart full dose or reintroduce one-by-one at 3-7 day intervals.
NephrotoxicityBUN/creatinine/urinalysis for signs of nephrotoxicity (oliguria under 30 mL/hr, edema) — not routine if asymptomatic without risk factorsDiscontinue Streptomycin if nephrotoxicity develops, refer to nephrology.
Nice To Know
  • Practical nuance from the lecturer: if the causative drug can't be discontinued and the patient has icteric sclera, difficulty eating, or nausea (the most common ADR symptoms), the usual approach is to stop and wait a bit, give silymarin and ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), repeat the labs, then rechallenge if the picture is acceptable.
  • Reintroduction sequence after a fixed-dose combination reaction (from the lecturer's cheat sheet): (1) remove the fixed-dose combination, (2) start with Isoniazid alone for 3 days and check for adverse reactions, (3) if none, add Rifampicin to Isoniazid for 3 days and check for drug interactions, rashes, and AST/ALT trend, (4) if no interactions/rash and AST/ALT have decreased, add Pyrazinamide or Ethambutol to Rifampicin+Isoniazid for 3 days, (5) if no adverse reactions, return to full HRZE dosing. This requires knowing the average daily dosage of each drug.
Mechanism — Drug Hypersensitivity Pathway
Drug exposure
↓
Delayed T-cell mediated reaction
↓
Cytotoxic T cells + cytokine release
↓
Tissue damage (DRESS/DIHS if eosinophilia + systemic symptoms present)
↓
STOP the medication
↓
Wait for AST/ALT/creatinine/uric acid to normalize AND symptoms to resolve
↓
Rechallenge (fewer doses, shorter) OR Desensitization (higher doses, longer — if rechallenge fails and drug cannot be dropped, not if SJS/TEN)
Recall Check
At what ALT elevation should all anti-TB drugs be stopped in a symptomatic patient?
More than 3 times the upper limit of normal.
At what ALT elevation should all anti-TB drugs be stopped in an asymptomatic patient?
More than 5 times the upper limit of normal.
After hepatotoxicity resolves, which drug is reintroduced first?
Rifampicin, followed by Isoniazid after 3 to 7 days.
Desensitization is contraindicated in which type of reaction?
Severe cutaneous reactions involving the mouth or mucous membranes, such as SJS or TEN.
Clinical Case Bank (Synchronous Session) p.7, 12, 14, 18, 20-21, 23 reviewed

All cases as presented in the lecture, condensed to question and answer. Use these as a final self-test after reviewing the drug-by-drug sections above.

Case 3 — Retreatment with Rifampicin Resistance (p.7)
JB, 34/M, previously treated with CAT I and CAT II, classified cured, returns with cough greater than 2 weeks. AFB 1+/1+, Gene Xpert: MTB detected, Rif resistance detected. What is this scenario testing?
This is the classic setup for suspecting and confirming drug-resistant TB in a retreatment case — Gene Xpert detecting rifampicin resistance means this is managed as Rifampicin-Resistant TB / MDR-TB and must be referred for programmatic PMDT management.
Clinical Case 1 — Choosing the Initial Regimen (p.14)
Julian Patrick, 24/M truck driver, 2-week history of productive cough, hemoptysis, low-grade fever, poor appetite, weight loss, reticulonodular opacities on right upper lobe, AFB +2. What regimen should be initiated?
Ethambutol, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Rifampicin (HRZE) — this is a new pulmonary TB case, so Category I treatment applies.
Clinical Case 2 — Isoniazid Target Molecule (p.18)
Bing-Bing, living with HIV, found to have latent TB, started on Isoniazid. The inhibitory effect is mediated by inhibition of which molecule?
Mycolic acid (not peptidoglycan, topoisomerase II, or DNA-dependent RNA polymerase — those describe other drugs).
Clinical Case 3 — Ototoxicity (p.20)
Ethan, on Category II treatment for 2 weeks, complains of hearing loss and ringing of the ears, no trauma history. Which drug is responsible?
Streptomycin.
Clinical Case 4 — Vitamin for Peripheral Neuropathy (p.20)
Christian, 17, on Category I treatment, complains of tingling sensation and heaviness in his limbs. Which drug/vitamin would best treat this?
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) — treating isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.
Clinical Case 5 — Aggravated Gout (p.21)
Timmy, 40, known gout, started anti-TB medications 2 months ago, now has acute gouty arthritis. Which drug most likely aggravated his gout?
Pyrazinamide.
Clinical Case 6 — Penetrates Phagocytic Cells (p.21)
Which anti-TB medication readily penetrates phagocytic cells and can kill organisms poorly accessible to other drugs, such as those in abscesses and lung cavities?
Rifampicin.
Clinical Case 7 — Resistance vs Mechanism of Action (p.21)
Which statement is true regarding the mechanism of RESISTANCE to antimycobacterial drugs — options included Isoniazid "expression of katG and inhA genes inhibits acid synthesis," Isoniazid "inhibits mycolic acid synthesis," Rifampicin "inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase," and Streptomycin "binds S12 ribosomal subunit inhibiting protein synthesis"?
The keyed answer is the Isoniazid resistance statement about katG/inhA gene changes — the other three options describe mechanism of ACTION, not resistance, which is the distinction the question is testing. Note: the exact wording of the keyed answer in the source ("expression of katG and inhA genes inhibits acid synthesis") is somewhat unclear as transcribed — it is reproduced here as written rather than smoothed over, since the PDF does not further clarify this phrasing.
Clinical Case 8 — Fluoroquinolone Mechanism (p.21)
Kinsley, 24/F, previously treated for PTB, again smear-positive. Which second-line medication acts via inhibition of bacterial topoisomerase and DNA gyrase?
Levofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone).
Clinical Case 9 — Oxazolidinone / VRSA (p.21)
Erika, newly diagnosed MDR/RR-TB, prescribed an oxazolidinone also used for vancomycin-resistant staphylococcus. What is its mechanism?
Inhibits binding of mycobacteria to the 23S subunit (Linezolid).
Clinical Case 10 — Hepatotoxicity Decision (p.23)
Krislyn, 16/F, started on anti-TB medications, develops rashes and abdominal pain after 1 week, AST/ALT are 3x baseline. What should be done?
Stop the treatment and observe — 3x elevation WITH symptoms meets the stop threshold (5x elevation would meet the threshold even without symptoms).
Clinical Case 11 — Breakthrough Seizures (p.23)
Hans, epilepsy, seizure-free for 2 years on phenobarbital, started on HRZE, then presents in status epilepticus. Which drug could have caused the breakthrough seizures?
Rifampicin — as a strong CYP450 enzyme inducer, it increases metabolism of phenobarbital (and other anticonvulsants like phenytoin/carbamazepine), lowering their levels and precipitating breakthrough seizures. This is the opposite direction of effect from Isoniazid, which instead inhibits metabolism of those same anticonvulsants.

Start building the regimen
├── STEP 1 → susceptible 1st-line agents (Z, E) + 1 Fluoroquinolone + 1 Injectable

Ask for: cough (any duration), unexplained fever, unexplained weight loss, night sweats — each lasting ≥2 weeks
├── 0 of these present → Chest X-ray
│ ├── CXR NOT suggestive of TB → consult for other diseases
│ └── CXR suggestive of TB → Presumptive TB
└── 1 or more present → Presumptive TB directly

Remove the fixed-dose combination
↓

Commonly Confused Concepts

Do Not Confuse: Rifampin vs Rifaximin
Rifampin
Defining feature: anti-TB / antimicrobial, inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Key clue: orange-red body fluids, strong CYP450 inducer.
Rifaximin
Defining feature: treats hepatic encephalopathy.
Key clue: works by decreasing ammoniagenic gut bacteria — not an anti-TB drug at all.
Fast distinction: same drug-name root, completely different clinical use — TB (rifampin) vs liver/ammonia (rifaximin).
Do Not Confuse: New Case vs Retreatment Case (and its subtypes)
New case
Defining feature: never treated for TB, or has taken TB drugs for less than 1 month.
Key clue: no meaningful treatment history.
Retreatment case
Defining feature: received at least 1 month of TB drugs in the past.
Key clue: further split into Relapse (completed treatment, recurrence), Treatment after failure (declared failed at month 5), TALF (interrupted 2 consecutive months), and PTOU (outcome unknown/undocumented).
Fast distinction: the 1-month treatment threshold is what separates "new" from "retreatment" — everything past that point is a flavor of retreatment.
Do Not Confuse: Monodrug-Resistant vs Poly-Drug-Resistant vs MDR-TB vs RR-TB
Monodrug-resistant TB
Resistant to exactly ONE first-line drug, and that drug is not rifampicin.
Poly-drug-resistant TB
Resistant to MORE THAN ONE first-line drug, but not to both rifampicin and isoniazid together.
MDR-TB
Resistant to AT LEAST isoniazid AND rifampicin together.
RR-TB (rifampicin-resistant)
Resistant to rifampicin, isoniazid sensitive or unknown — but WHO treats RR-TB the same as MDR-TB for regimen purposes.
Fast distinction: ask "how many drugs, and does it include BOTH isoniazid and rifampicin?" — that answers which category applies.
Do Not Confuse: Rechallenge vs Desensitization
Rechallenge
Defining feature: progressive dosing to verify no immediate reaction.
Key clue: fewer doses, shorter duration, more commonly used in the Philippines.
Desensitization
Defining feature: rapid incremental dosing to induce drug tolerance.
Key clue: higher doses, longer duration, contraindicated in SJS/TEN or mucosal involvement.
Fast distinction: rechallenge is the everyday first attempt, desensitization is the fallback used when rechallenge fails and the drug truly cannot be dropped.
Do Not Confuse: Isoniazid's Enzyme Effect vs Rifampicin's Enzyme Effect
Isoniazid
Defining feature: INHIBITS hepatic metabolism of phenytoin, carbamazepine, diazepam, triazolam, clofazimine, cycloserine, warfarin.
Key clue: co-administered drug LEVELS RISE → toxicity risk.
Rifampicin
Defining feature: INDUCES (CYP3A4) metabolism of many drugs including phenytoin, carbamazepine, OCPs, steroids, anticoagulants.
Key clue: co-administered drug LEVELS FALL → subtherapeutic effect / breakthrough symptoms (e.g. Clinical Case 11's breakthrough seizures on phenobarbital).
Fast distinction: Isoniazid raises other drugs' levels (inhibition), Rifampicin lowers them (induction) — opposite directions, easy to mix up on an exam.
Do Not Confuse: Streptomycin vs Pyrazinamide (opposite niches)
Streptomycin
Extracellular bacilli only, alkaline pH, given IM, never crosses the BBB.
Pyrazinamide
Intracellular (inside macrophage lysosomes), acidic pH, oral, penetrates CSF well.
Fast distinction: these two occupy opposite ends of the location/pH spectrum among first-line-adjacent drugs.
Do Not Confuse: Delamanid vs Pretomanid
Delamanid
Nitroimidazooxazole, activated by enzyme Rv3547.
Pretomanid
Nitroimidazooxazine (Delamanid's "cousin" per the lecturer), part of BPaLM.
Fast distinction: both inhibit mycolic acid synthesis and share isoniazid/ethambutol-like toxicity (peripheral/optic neuropathy), but only Pretomanid is part of the BPaLM regimen in this lecture.
8

Exam Traps

Exam trap

Pyrazinamide raises uric acid in essentially every patient. Hyperuricemia alone is not a reason to stop the drug — only symptomatic gouty arthritis is. A question that describes "elevated uric acid, no symptoms" on PZA is testing whether you'll incorrectly stop the drug.

Exam trap

A patient stable on an anticonvulsant (phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) who starts HRZE and then has breakthrough seizures — the culprit is usually Rifampicin, because it INDUCES hepatic metabolism and lowers anticonvulsant levels. Isoniazid does the opposite (inhibits metabolism, raises anticonvulsant levels toward toxicity) — don't reverse these two in your head.

Exam trap

Bacteriological confirmation of PTB requires only ONE positive sputum AFB smear where EQA is established — a question implying "you need at least two positive smears" is testing this exact point, and is incorrect per the source guideline.

Exam trap

Routine liver function tests and serum uric acid are NOT requested before or during TB treatment in asymptomatic patients without risk factors. Testing is triggered by symptoms (jaundice, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain for LFTs, or gouty joint pain for uric acid) — not done "just in case."

Exam trap

Ethambutol is contraindicated in pre-existing optic neuritis from any cause, not only optic neuritis caused by ethambutol itself — a history of optic neuritis from any etiology should raise a flag before starting this drug.

Exam trap

Food timing matters differently across the four first-line drugs. Isoniazid and Rifampicin both have reduced bioavailability with food (take empty stomach) — Rifampicin's is reduced by about 30%. Pyrazinamide's absorption is unaffected by food. A question mixing up which drug is food-sensitive is testing this exact distinction.

Exam trap

In HIV patients on TB treatment, Efavirenz is the preferred NNRTI. Nevirapine is avoided due to drug-drug interactions. If a question asks which NNRTI is safe alongside HRZE, the answer is Efavirenz, not Nevirapine.

Exam trap

Renal dose adjustment is drug-specific, not a blanket rule for all anti-TB drugs. Isoniazid and Rifampicin generally do not need dose adjustment in renal failure or hemodialysis (aside from timing). Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin/aminoglycosides do need adjustment (reduced dose and/or less frequent dosing) in renal impairment.

Exam trap

Isoniazid monotherapy is acceptable only for latent TB (low bacillary load) — never for active TB disease, where monotherapy of any single drug risks selecting out resistant organisms. Don't let a vignette about "active TB" tempt you toward a single-drug answer.

Exam trap

Desensitization is contraindicated in severe cutaneous reactions with mouth/mucous membrane involvement (SJS, TEN). If a vignette describes mucosal involvement, rechallenge/desensitization is not simply "pick whichever" — desensitization specifically is off the table.

Exam trap

The PDF explicitly warns: exam questions will specify if the treatment basis is WHO guidelines. If a question does not say so, default to DOH National TB Control Program Guidelines — this changes which regimen (for example 2HRZE/4HR vs 2HPZM/2HPM) is the "correct" answer.

9

Rapid-Fire Final Recall

Quick-answer prompts covering the whole lesson. Click to reveal each answer.

Causative organism of TB?
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slow-growing AFB.
Who first isolated it, and when?
Robert Koch, 1882.
The 4 current first-line drugs?
Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide.
Which classic first-line drug was removed from the first-line list?
Streptomycin.
DOH Category I regimen for new PTB?
2HRZE/4HR.
Enzyme that activates isoniazid?
KatG (mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase).
Isoniazid's ultimate molecular target?
InhA — blocking mycolic acid synthesis.
Main gene mutation for isoniazid resistance?
katG (also inhA overexpression, kasA, ahpC).
Rifampicin's molecular target?
The β-subunit of RNA polymerase, gene rpoB.
Rifampicin's hallmark pharmacologic property?
Strong CYP450 (CYP3A4) enzyme inducer.
Enzyme that activates pyrazinamide?
Pyrazinamidase, gene pncA.
pH at which pyrazinamide is active?
Acidic (about 5.5) — inactive at neutral pH.
Most hepatotoxic of the first-line drugs?
Pyrazinamide.
Ethambutol's molecular target?
Arabinosyl transferase, embCAB operon.
Ethambutol's hallmark toxicity?
Optic/retrobulbar neuritis with red-green color blindness.
Which first-line drug is bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal (by default classification)?
Ethambutol.
Streptomycin's route?
IM only — not absorbed orally.
Streptomycin's two hallmark toxicities?
Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
Vitamin given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy?
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).
ALT threshold to stop all TB drugs if the patient IS symptomatic?
More than 3 times the upper limit of normal.
ALT threshold to stop all TB drugs if the patient is asymptomatic?
More than 5 times the upper limit of normal.
Which drug is reintroduced first after hepatotoxicity resolves?
Rifampicin, then Isoniazid 3-7 days later.
Definition of MDR-TB?
Resistant to at least isoniazid AND rifampicin.
How does WHO manage RR-TB (rifampicin-resistant)?
The same as MDR-TB.
Required initial test for presumptive DR-TB?
Xpert MTB/RIF.
WHO group containing the fluoroquinolones?
Group A.
WHO group containing Bedaquiline and Delamanid?
Group D, specifically D2.
The new 6-month, all-oral MDR-TB regimen (2024 update)?
BPaLM — Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin.
The only ART regimen safe with the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen?
An efavirenz-containing regimen.
Preferred NNRTI in HIV patients on TB treatment?
Efavirenz (avoid Nevirapine).
When does ART start relative to TB treatment, in ordinary (non-meningitis) TB?
After the 2nd week of TB treatment, regardless of CD4.
When does ART start in TB meningitis?
After the intensive phase of TB treatment (first 2 months).
Prophylactic antibiotic given to all PLHIV on TB treatment regardless of CD4?
Co-trimoxazole (800/160), for PCP prophylaxis.
Which drug is swapped out for Streptomycin in compensated liver cirrhosis regimens?
Pyrazinamide.
Which drug among those covered is contraindicated in pregnancy AND lactation?
Streptomycin (Ethionamide is also teratogenic/contraindicated in pregnancy).
Rechallenge vs desensitization — which uses fewer doses over a shorter time?
Rechallenge.
What contraindicates desensitization?
Severe cutaneous reaction with mouth/mucosal involvement — SJS, TEN.
Linezolid's ribosomal target?
The 50S subunit (23S rRNA portion).
Bedaquiline's molecular target?
Mycobacterial ATP synthase.
What drug class does linezolid belong to?
Oxazolidinone.

Last-Minute Cram Sheet (5-Minute Read)

Definitions

  • Bacteriologically confirmed TB = 1 positive AFB smear, culture, or Xpert MTB/RIF is enough.
  • MDR-TB = resistant to isoniazid AND rifampicin. RR-TB is managed the same way.
  • New case = never treated or under 1 month of treatment. Everything else is some form of retreatment.

The Four First-Line Drugs, One Line Each

  • Isoniazid — prodrug, KatG activates it, blocks mycolic acid synthesis via InhA, bactericidal, give with pyridoxine.
  • Rifampicin — blocks RNA polymerase (rpoB), bactericidal, strong enzyme inducer, orange body fluids.
  • Pyrazinamide — prodrug, pncA activates it, only works in acid/intracellular, most hepatotoxic, hyperuricemia expected.
  • Ethambutol — blocks arabinogalactan synthesis (embCAB), bacteriostatic, watch for optic neuritis / red-green color blindness.

Regimens

  • New drug-sensitive case → 2HRZE/4HR (DOH default unless a question specifies WHO).
  • MDR/RR-TB, newest WHO option → BPaLM x 6 months, all oral (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid + Moxifloxacin).
  • 4-month option for non-drug-resistant PTB → Rifapentine + Moxifloxacin based (2HPZM/2HPM), only with efavirenz-based ART if HIV+.

Adverse Effect Stop-Rules

  • Hepatotoxicity: stop ALL drugs if ALT >3x ULN with symptoms, or >5x ULN even without symptoms.
  • Visual change → stop Ethambutol. Hearing/vestibular change → stop Streptomycin. Gouty arthritis → stop Pyrazinamide.
  • Reintroduction order after hepatotoxicity resolves: Rifampicin first, then Isoniazid.

Contraindications to Remember

  • Streptomycin — contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation.
  • Ethambutol — avoid in pre-existing optic neuritis and in young children who can't reliably report vision changes.
  • Desensitization — contraindicated in SJS/TEN or mucosal involvement.
  • Ethionamide — teratogenic, avoid in pregnancy.

Classic Associations

  • Efavirenz = safe NNRTI with TB treatment. Nevirapine = avoid.
  • Compensated liver cirrhosis regimen swaps out Pyrazinamide for Streptomycin.
  • Hemodialysis patients get anti-TB drugs right after their dialysis session.
  • Bedaquiline and Delamanid both need a baseline ECG (QT prolongation).

Essential Exceptions and Traps

  • PZA-induced hyperuricemia is expected — not a reason to stop by itself.
  • Isoniazid inhibits metabolism of other drugs (levels rise). Rifampicin induces metabolism (levels fall) — opposite directions, classic trap (see Clinical Case 11's breakthrough seizures on Rifampicin).
  • Isoniazid monotherapy is fine for latent TB only, never for active disease.
  • Routine LFTs and uric acid are NOT checked unless symptoms or risk factors are present.
